Jordan Blake - Send security pack (SOC 2, ISO certs, pen test summary) and link to audit log retention options (due: 2026-07-23)

header: Date: 2026-07-22 | Start: 15:00 PDT | Duration: 54m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Aisha (CS), Ravi (SE) — Maya (Cobalt SecOps), Liam (Cobalt SRE), Priya (Cobalt Legal), Ethan (Infra)
summary: Cobalt Energy and Redwood reviewed the incident response playbook, KMS residency and encryption options, RBAC/SSO integration, audit log retention, and SLA/BCDR targets (RTO/RPO). Key outcomes: alignment on draft RTO 15m / RPO 5m target for critical inference endpoints, action items to share playbook artifacts and runbook snippets, and plan for an on-site KMS integration review.
topics: KMS / encryption residency (cloud KMS vs customer-managed HSM)
RBAC / SSO SAML flows and SCIM provisioning
SLA uptime, credits, and escalation paths
transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to walk through the incident playbook and specifically KMS residency because I know Cobalt has some strong residency requirements. uh so we'll go through the runbook, escalation steps and the RTO/RPO targets.
[00:00:18] Maya: thanks Jordan, appreciate it. we have a few constraints — power grid control plane uptime is critical and our legal team is very strict on key custody. Priya will chime in on that side.
[00:00:30] Priya: hi all, yes the big ask is we need provable separation of keys and audit trail for any crypto ops, ideally customer-managed HSM with attestable key access logs.
[00:00:45] Samir: totally, we can support multiple KMS patterns. topologies we've seen: 1) Redwood-managed KMS (cloud provider), 2) Redwood-integrated customer KMS (bring-your-own KMS via external key wrap), 3) direct HSM bridging in private deployments. each has tradeoffs for latency and operational overhead.
[00:01:10] Liam: when you say key wrap, do you mean the keys are always in our HSM and you never have plaintext on your side?
[00:01:18] Samir: correct — with external key wrap the master key stays in your HSM, we receive wrapped keys and decrypt only within a controlled enclave or never see plaintext for sensitive material. there's a few implementation nuances depending on private vs hosted.
[00:01:33] Ethan: latency wise, any KMS call on token generation adds... what is the typical 90th percentile?
[00:01:41] Ravi: on hosted we see sub-20ms for cloud-provider KMS in the same region; external HSM across peered VPCs can be 40-120ms depending on network hops — we do caching to avoid per-token roundtrips and also support local key cache with rewrap intervals.
[00:01:59] Maya: hmm caching is fine but we need clear TTLs and rotation/compromise procedures. if a key is rotated we need guarantees on revocation across all nodes.
[00:02:12] Samir: agreed. our runtime supports immediate revocation signals; we push a revocation event and nodes check the revocation list within the configured window — we can make that window auditable.
[00:02:26] Jordan: stepping back to incident playbook — table of contents we covered: detection, triage, containment, mitigation, communication. how do we escalate from SEV1 to executive? what's the timeline?
[00:02:38] Maya: Cobalt expects exec notification within 30 minutes of confirmed service-impacting incident.
[00:02:44] Jordan: okay we can align that. our standard is page on SEV1 within 15 minutes to on-call, and exec notification for a confirmed customer-impacting incident within 30 minutes; we can document the exact contact list.
[00:02:58] Liam: RTO targets — you mentioned earlier defaults, can you restate?
[00:03:04] Samir: for dedicated/private customers we generally offer SLO guidance: critical inference endpoints RTO 15m, RPO 5m assuming KV cache checkpoints and replication enabled. non-critical background jobs have longer windows. these are engineering targets we validate in tabletop and DR drills.
[00:03:19] Priya: is that guaranteed in contract or just an internal target?
[00:03:24] Jordan: contractually we typically offer SLA availability numbers (e.g., 99.95%) with credits; RTO/RPO are operational commitments we can bake into an SOW for Dedicated/Private customers. for hosted tier it's more advisory unless there's a custom enterprise SLA.
[00:03:40] Ethan: what about audit logs — tamper-evident, retention, who can read them?
[00:03:48] Aisha: logs are written to an append-only store with integrity checks; for private deployments logs can be pushed to your SIEM or stored in a customer-controlled S3 bucket. retention is configurable — default 90 days; we have options up to 7 years for legal requirements. read access is controlled via RBAC and can be limited to a small admin group.
[00:04:06] Maya: does the append-only store provide proof of non-repudiation? timestamps and chain-of-hash?
[00:04:12] Samir: we support hash chaining and periodic signed manifests for tamper-evidence; we can provide verification tooling.
[00:04:20] Jordan: quick note — Priya asked about SOC 2 evidence. we'll share recent SOC 2 report excerpt and pen test summary after the call.
[00:04:28] Priya: thanks. also for SSO, Cobalt uses Okta and wants SCIM provisioning and SAML SSO — do you support SCIM for user sync and role mapping?
[00:04:36] Ravi: yes SCIM v2 supported, and we map SCIM groups to role templates. we also have customizable RBAC so you can lock certain actions to a security admin role.
[00:04:48] Maya: a point on least privilege — we need read-only access for audit teams and more restricted keys for ops.
[00:04:55] Samir: understood. roles are configurable and we can propose a baseline RBAC policy for Cobalt.
[00:05:02] Jordan: moving to escalation channels — email, Slack, PagerDuty, and phone tree — what's Redwood's typical on-call?
[00:05:09] Ravi: 24/7 on-call with primary/secondary, and an escalation to engineering shift leads. exec paging only on extended incidents. we integrate with PagerDuty and can tie runbook steps to PD playbooks.
[00:05:20] Liam: would we be able to trigger automatic failover to a cold region or degraded mode to keep inference online? that's key for us.
[00:05:28] Samir: yes we have graceful degradation: model fallback to a quantized variant, reduce throughput to preserve latency, and cross-region failover. failover strategy is configurable by route and can be automated or manual.
[00:05:44] Maya: okay let's talk verification — how do you prove RTO/RPO in a tabletop? do you run end-to-end failovers?
[00:05:52] Samir: we run scheduled drills with synthetic traffic and smoke tests. for private customers we can run joint drills where we cut a region and measure time to restoration. we publish a drill report with timestamps and lessons learned.
[00:06:08] Jordan: Samir will attach a sample drill report after this call.
[00:06:12] Priya: question on encryption in transit — IDS/IPS monitoring for key exchanges?
[00:06:17] Samir: all control plane comms are TLS 1.3, mutual TLS for private links; we can optionally enable network-level IDS/IPS for private deployments and share alerts into your SOC.
[00:06:29] Maya: auditability of admin actions — if a Redwood engineer escalates and performs a hotfix, how is that tracked?
[00:06:35] Aisha: we log all admin console actions, we require SSO and MFA for access, and privilege elevation is ticketed. we can produce an audit export that ties actions to user identity and time.
[00:06:46] Ethan: you mentioned privilege elevation — do you support break-glass with timeboxed keys?
[00:06:51] Samir: yes, we have time-bound elevation tokens with approvals and we record the session for audit.
[00:06:58] Liam: can we get an on-prem installer that uses our HSM for key ops?
[00:07:03] Ravi: we offer an on-prem package for regulated environments; key ops can be configured to use your HSM via PKCS#11 or cloud HSM bridges. we'll need network details for peering and bandwidth tests.
[00:07:15] Maya: great. one more thing on data residency — inference logs sometimes contain PII in prompts, how do you handle prompt retention?
[00:07:25] Samir: we support configurable prompt retention and redaction at ingestion; for Private deployments you control retention. for hosted we have retention settings and options for prompt masking and redaction rules.
[00:07:38] Jordan: switching gears to SLA credits — our standard SLA is 99.95% for critical endpoints which maps to X minutes of downtime a month; credits are pro-rated. we can include higher guarantees in enterprise contracts.
[00:07:52] Priya: what's your mean time to acknowledge?
[00:07:56] Ravi: primary on-call acknowledges within 5-15 minutes; that's part of our runbook.
[00:08:02] Maya: walk me through the escalation path in your playbook for a SEV1 where keys are suspected compromised.
[00:08:08] Samir: step 1: immediate containment — revoke wrapped keys, spin up fallback keys, promote cached keys; step 2: notify customer and security contacts; step 3: snapshot logs and forensics; step 4: if keys compromised we trigger full key rotation and node re-encrypt. the timeline for containment is expected within 15 minutes with our cached key window.
[00:08:31] Priya: what about forensic artifacts — do you transfer chain-of-custody to us?
[00:08:36] Aisha: yes we prepare a forensic bundle and we can hand over logs with hashes and signed manifests. we also keep an internal copy for RCA.
[00:08:47] Liam: how do you test the key revocation path without impacting production?
[00:08:52] Samir: we run a staged drill using canary routes and simulated traffic, with a small percent of traffic diverted to a test rig; we validate revocation and failback, then widen scope.
[00:09:05] Maya: ok good. now the customer wants explicit RPO math — how are you getting 5 minutes?
[00:09:11] Samir: it's based on KV checkpoint frequency and replication latency. with checkpointing every 2 minutes and replication to a warm standby, worst-case rollback is the time since last checkpoint plus ingestion buffering — typically under 5 minutes for critical endpoints.
[00:09:28] Ethan: any single points of failure in the control plane?
[00:09:31] Ravi: control plane is multi-AZ with leader election and failover; state is replicated with consensus (raft-like). we have multi-region orchestration for large customers.
[00:09:41] Jordan: let's capture a few concrete asks so we don't miss them. first: sample playbook with the SEV definitions and the exec notify timeline. second: sample SOC2 artifacts and pen test summary. third: HSM integration checklist and network diagram.
[00:09:56] Priya: and a written statement on data residency and prompt retention options for legal review.
[00:10:01] Aisha: we will compile those into a security pack.
[00:10:05] Maya: are there any customer examples of similar KMS integrations?
[00:10:09] Samir: yes we've done similar for a utility provider in EMEA — we can anonymize and share a readout.
[00:10:15] Jordan: quick technical deep dive, if that's ok — Samir you wanna show the revocation flow?
[00:10:19] Samir: sure. so diagram: app -> Redwood edge -> runtime nodes; keys are cached at runtime with TTL and a revocation feed from central KMS. revocation feed is gossiped and nodes will check signature and invalidate keys. we store audit logs separately and sign manifests every hour.
[00:10:40] Liam: how often is the manifest signed? hourly is fine but legal may ask for daily signed buckets for long term retention.
[00:10:47] Samir: we can produce daily and hourly if needed.
[00:10:51] Jordan: ok we're getting close to time. let's recap next steps — Samir will prepare runbook snippets and a drill sample; Jordan will send SOC2 and security pack; Cobalt to share their RTO acceptance and escalation matrix.
[00:11:04] Maya: yes and we'll book the on-site week of Aug 10 for the KMS integration review.
[00:11:10] Priya: one last legal ask — can you confirm you support contract language for key custody and attestations?
[00:11:16] Jordan: yes we can include key custody language and attestations in the SOW for private deployments; we'll draft starter language.
[00:11:24] Jordan: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the next workshop.
[00:11:30] [END OF RECORDED TRANSCRIPT - remaining meeting minutes were a separate breakout for network folks not recorded by main recorder]
